description: We are Apollo, a passionate and creative team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We bring together diverse skills in software development, artificial intelligence, design, research, and storytelling to transform forgotten space equipment into meaningful stories. Our goal is to combine technology, creativity, and scientific thinking to explore the legacy of NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars.
summary:
OPPY: The Last Signal is a first-person 3D exploration game, playable in a web browser, that brings one piece of NASA's off-world hardware back to life: the Opportunity rover, which has stood silent in Perseverance Valley on Mars since 2018.

The challenge asks for a story that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to hardware left across the solar system and the science it made possible. We chose one machine and told its whole story from its own point of view. The player is an astronaut following a mysterious signal along Opportunity's route: Eagle Crater, Endurance Crater, Victoria Crater, the rim of Endeavour Crater, and Perseverance Valley. At each site, they find a piece of the rover's hardware (its landing platform, arm instruments, camera, a wheel, a solar panel) and recover a "memory" narrated by Opportunity, each tied to a real discovery or engineering problem. The journey ends at the rover itself.

It matters because Opportunity's story is usually a list of dates. We wanted young players to walk it and to finish feeling they know this machine: built for 90 days, it worked for more than 14 years and found evidence that water once persisted on Mars. A playthrough takes about ten minutes and needs no install.

The hardware and its science are real; the signal, the astronaut, and the rover's voice are fiction, and the game says so on screen.
details:
How does it address the challenge?

The hardware is the cast. Each checkpoint presents one real component and what it did: the airbag lander that delivered the rover, the arm's rock-grinding tool and spectrometers, the panoramic camera, the wheels, the solar panels.

Engineering is linked to science. The arm memory explains how grinding into layered rock revealed repeated wetting by water; the wheel memory covers driving with damaged hardware and reaching gypsum and clay deposits; the solar panel memory explains why a dust storm ended the mission.

It shows instead of listing. Facts arrive as narrated memories at the place they happened, and each one unlocks a mission-log entry with the historical context.

Audience: school-age students and casual space fans. Subtitles accompany every voiced line.

How it works? 

Opening: a mission control room where the signal appears on the wall screen, then a camera descent onto the landing site.

Exploration: first-person walking on Mars. A helmet-style compass shows the signal as a soft arc that sharpens as the player closes in.

Six checkpoints in historical order, each with a voiced memory while the camera circles the artifact.

Finale: haze thickens toward Perseverance Valley to echo the 2018 dust storm, and the ending shows real mission achievements.

Honesty layer: an on-screen note states whether the ground underfoot is real elevation data or simulated, and an About panel separates fact from fiction.

Tools:

React, TypeScript, Vite; Three.js with custom GLSL shaders.

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Pillow) to prepare HiRISE terrain offline.

A Node.js script to generate voice-over offline.

Static site hosted on Vercel; source on GitHub.

Limitations: 

Only Victoria Crater uses measured terrain, shown at half size. Other terrain is procedurally generated and distances are heavily compressed.

Five of the six artifacts are simple placeholder shapes; the rover is NASA's 3D model.

The artifacts are symbolic. Opportunity did not leave parts along its route.
